metadata.title: Finding an Unknown Capital from Profit Shares
metadata.description: Recover a missing contribution or initial capital by comparing its weighted share with known partners.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the capital-time model step by step; use timelines and segment ledgers; show intermediate calculations, unit and share checks, and topic-specific remedial feedback. Practice uses fresh values aligned to the approved scope.
metadata.sourceScope: R. S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude, Chapter 14: Partnership (printed pp. 476–492). Approved scope: Set known and unknown capital-time products in the ratio of the partners’ profit shares, then solve for the missing capital. Include an unknown initial contribution when an investment is later increased or reduced, and cases where a partner’s stated share is a fraction of total profit. Check the solved capital is positive and substitute it into the full multi-partner ratio. Ground in solved examples 12–13 and objective patterns 37, 43–45, 49, 51–53, and 64.

content.text: Finding an Unknown Capital from Profit Shares: Recover a missing contribution or initial capital by comparing its weighted share with known partners. This lesson builds a partnership model, explains each step, works through examples, and offers fresh practice with targeted recovery.

Finding an Unknown Capital from Profit Shares asks you to decide what determines each partner’s share. Recover a missing contribution or initial capital by comparing its weighted share with known partners. We will build the model from the agreement, calculate a representative case, and test the result against the original conditions.

Start with the quantity the agreement actually rewards. In ordinary partnership profit sharing, that is the capital made available to the business over time. When a partner’s capital is unknown, the known profit ratio determines its missing capital-time weight. Write the partner names and the stated basis before you choose an operation.

The core model is: each partner’s weight = capital × time invested. This follows by comparing equal units of capital-month: twice the capital for the same duration contributes twice as much, and the same capital held twice as long also contributes twice as much.

Use C₁t₁:C₂t₂=p:q, then solve for the missing capital. If capital changes during the year, first calculate the partner’s total segmented weight. Keep the capital amount and its time period in separate columns first. Only multiply once both are expressed in compatible units; this makes the origin of every ratio term visible.

Worked reasoning: A invests ₹20,000 for 12 months. B invests x for 8 months and their profit ratio is 3:2. Then 240,000:8x=3:2, so x=₹20,000. Notice that the ratio comes from relative contribution, not from the order in which partners are named or from who manages the business. Preserve the labels until the final allocation.

When the total profit is known, add the reduced ratio terms to find total parts. Divide the distributable profit by those parts for one part, then multiply by the requested partner’s parts. Do not treat a ratio term itself as a rupee amount.

Use the timeline or agreement to identify intervals before doing arithmetic. Separate the ratio step from the arithmetic step to avoid dropping a duration. If a partner’s capital changes, record the new amount only from the date it takes effect; if a time factor is common to everyone, cancel it only after forming the ratio.

A second way to check the model is to rebuild each partner’s contribution independently. Check the positive capital and substitute it into the weighted ratio; if other partners exist, include their weights when interpreting a total share. If the resulting ratio reverses a known relationship—for example, a larger weighted contribution receiving a smaller share—inspect the partner labels and ratio order.

Watch for this error: A share fraction alone does not determine the capital unless the comparison partner’s weight or the total ratio is known. Another frequent slip is to use elapsed time instead of invested time. Mark the start and end of each interval; for a late entrant in a T-month business, invested duration is T minus the delay.

A useful worked check is to allocate the full pool and add the receipts. For partner i, the share is total profit × (i’s weight / all partners’ weights). This fraction must be between 0 and 1 for positive weights, and all partner fractions must sum to 1.

Translate special wording before calculation. A percentage increase may refer to original capital, a withdrawal may be partial, and an allowance may be removed before investment-based sharing. If the profit share is given as a fraction of total profit, convert it to a ratio against the remaining partners. Underline the base of each percentage and state whether the pool is original or remaining profit.

If an unknown amount or date is requested, set up the relationship before solving. Equate the capital-time products in the stated profit ratio, or write a share as its fraction of total profit. Keep unknowns tied to their partner labels and check that a date remains within the business term.

If your first answer seems wrong, revisit the model rather than repeating the arithmetic. Ask: did I use the right basis, include every interval, convert all time units, and use the right total pool? Then substitute the candidate into the original data and recompute the ratio.

For a timed exam, use a compact ledger: partner; capital in each interval; months in that interval; weighted contribution; share fraction. Reduce large products by common factors only after they are formed, and keep exact fractions until the final currency amount.

Mastery check: explain why the chosen weights represent the agreement, show one intermediate calculation, and verify the final share or sufficiency conclusion. You should now be able to solve the approved scope for finding an unknown capital from profit shares without relying on a memorized answer pattern.
Model the named partners and the profit pool before calculating. The profit ratio compares capital-time products, not capital alone. Keep every capital, duration, and change attached to its partner.
A invests ₹20000 for 12 months; B invests for 8 months. If their profit shares are 3:2, find B's capital.

inlineData.prompt: A invests ₹20000 for 12 months; B invests for 8 months. If their profit shares are 3:2, find B's capital.
hints: The profit ratio compares capital-time products, not capital alone.
inlineData.explanation: Set (20000×12):(C_B×8)=3:2. Hence C_B=20000×12×2/(3×8)=20000, so B's capital is ₹20000. Substitute to confirm the capital-time ratio.
